ISED B-001-023-001

Which of these statements about the installation or modification of an antenna structure is NOT correct?

False statement to select: An amateur radio operator may erect any size antenna structure without consulting neighbours or the local land-use authority

This is false. Consult the applicable local/ISED process and determine whether a defined exclusion applies. Amateur certification is not an unconditional permission for structures of any size.

ISED B-001-023-002

Who has authority over antenna installations, including antenna masts and towers?

Correct answer: The Minister of Innovation, Science and Industry

ISED B-001-023-003

When may you NOT be required to contact land-use authorities to determine public consultation requirements for an antenna system?

Correct answer: When an exclusion criterion defined by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada applies

ISED B-001-023-004

If an amateur radio operator wants to install or modify an antenna system and the local land-use authority has no approval process, what must the amateur radio operator do?

Correct answer: Follow the default public consultation process outlined by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada

ISED B-001-023-005

Which is NOT an element of the Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada public consultation process for antenna systems?

Item not required by this process: Participating in public meetings on the project

The question asks for the item that is NOT a required element of the default process. Written notice, a comment opportunity and responding to reasonable/relevant concerns are required; a public meeting is not automatically required.

ISED B-001-023-006

Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's default public consultation process for antenna systems requires proponents to address:

Correct answer: reasonable and relevant concerns provided in writing within the 30-day public comment period

ISED B-001-023-007

In a municipality with a public consultation process for antenna systems, when might public consultation NOT be required?

Correct answer: The system is excluded by the municipal process OR the provisions of Client Procedures Circular CPC-2-0-03

ISED B-001-023-008

The proponent of an antenna system and a stakeholder, other than the general public, have failed to reach an agreement. How is a final decision reached?

Correct answer: The decision is made by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada

Ignoring other requirements regarding the installation or modification of an antenna system, what is the tallest antenna structure you could erect without public consultation?

Correct answer: The tallest exempted by the land-use authority or Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada

ISED B-001-023-010

Where a land-use authority or municipality has established a public consultation process for antenna systems, who determines how public consultation should take place?

Correct answer: The municipality or local land-use authority

lessons.title: What Safety Code 6 actually limits
lessons.teachingSummary: Health Canada publishes Safety Code 6 for human exposure to RF fields. ISED applies the relevant requirements to transmitting installations. Its limits concern exposure—such as electric/magnetic fields, induced/contact currents and specific absorption rate—not simply a single allowed number of transmitter watts.
lessons.teaching:
Health Canada publishes Safety Code 6 for human exposure to RF fields. ISED applies the relevant requirements to transmitting installations. Its limits concern exposure—such as electric/magnetic fields, induced/contact currents and specific absorption rate—not simply a single allowed number of transmitter watts.

The exam identifies 48–300 MHz as a region of high whole-body absorption and low permitted exposure, and nerve stimulation as another established concern, especially below 10 MHz. Controlled and uncontrolled environments have different limits, with lower public exposure limits for uncontrolled areas.

No class of transmitter, including handhelds, is simply excluded from the requirements. There is no universal maximum safe handheld antenna power stated as a single wattage in the question. Antenna gain, frequency, distance, duty cycle and the physical arrangement affect exposure. The bank's claims that handhelds are excluded or that the code merely caps power fed into antennas are false statements selected in NOT-correct questions.

Use the applicable current assessment method for a real station. A low SWR or an amateur certificate does not demonstrate RF-exposure compliance.

ISED B-001-024-001

What organization has published safety guidelines for the maximum limits of RF energy near the human body?

Correct answer: Health Canada

ISED B-001-024-002

What is the purpose of Safety Code 6?

Correct answer: It gives RF exposure limits for the human body

ISED B-001-024-003

According to Safety Code 6, what frequencies cause us the greatest risk from RF energy?

Correct answer: 48 MHz to 300 MHz

ISED B-001-024-004

Why is the limit of exposure to RF the lowest in the frequency range of 48 MHz to 300 MHz, according to Safety Code 6?

Correct answer: The human body absorbs RF energy the most in this range

ISED B-001-024-005

According to Safety Code 6, what is the maximum safe power output to the antenna of a hand-held VHF or UHF radio?

Correct answer: Not specified

ISED B-001-024-006

When specifying maximum levels of exposure to RF fields, which two basic situations does Safety Code 6 cover?

Correct answer: Controlled and uncontrolled environments

ISED B-001-024-007

Apart from energy absorption and especially below 10 MHz, what is the second established adverse health effect described in Safety Code 6?

Correct answer: Nerve stimulation

ISED B-001-024-008

Which statement is NOT correct?

False statement to select: Hand-held transmitters are excluded from Safety Code 6 requirements

This statement is false: handheld transmitters are not excluded from RF-exposure requirements. Exposure depends on the actual operating arrangement, not just the equipment category.

ISED B-001-024-009

Safety Code 6 sets limits for RF exposure from radio transmitters. Which types of transmitters are exempt from regulation?

Correct answer: No transmitters are exempt

ISED B-001-024-010

Which of these statements about Safety Code 6 is NOT correct?

False statement to select: Safety Code 6 sets limits in terms of power levels fed into antennas

This is false. Safety Code 6 limits exposure quantities, such as fields, currents and energy absorption. Transmitter watts alone do not determine exposure.

lessons.title: Electrical hazards and preventing unauthorized use
lessons.teachingSummary: Keep unqualified people from using a station unsupervised: the bank suggests a key-operated main power switch at home and removing the microphone from an unused mobile station. A vehicle battery's major electrical hazard is its high short-circuit current, which can heat wiring and start fires despite the nominal 12-V supply.
lessons.teaching:
Keep unqualified people from using a station unsupervised: the bank suggests a key-operated main power switch at home and removing the microphone from an unused mobile station. A vehicle battery's major electrical hazard is its high short-circuit current, which can heat wiring and start fires despite the nominal 12-V supply.

High-voltage equipment should have appropriate interlocks. Before investigating a mains supply, turn it off and unplug it, then address stored charge using safe procedures. Working live creates an electric-shock risk; the heart can be affected by very small currents.

The bank asks for 20 mA as its minimum potentially fatal current and 30 V as a voltage usually considered hazardous. These are examination figures, not boundaries below which every exposure is safe; current path, contact conditions and duration matter. Do not use them to justify touching energized equipment.

If someone is in contact with a dangerous source, de-energize it before touching them, call emergency help and provide appropriate first aid when safe. Prevent becoming a second casualty.

ISED B-003-018-001

How could you best keep unauthorized persons from using your station at home?

Correct answer: Use a key-operated on/off switch in the main power line

ISED B-003-018-002

How could you best keep unauthorized persons from using a mobile station in your car?

Correct answer: Remove the microphone when you are not using it

ISED B-003-018-003

What electrical hazard, if any, does the starter battery in a vehicle present?

Correct answer: High short-circuit current

ISED B-003-018-004

Why would there be a switch in a high-voltage power supply to turn off the power if its cabinet is opened?

Correct answer: To keep anyone opening the cabinet from getting shocked by dangerous high voltages

ISED B-003-018-005

What is the minimum electrical current that can be fatal to the human body?

Correct answer: 20 milliamperes

ISED B-003-018-006

Which body organ can be fatally affected by a very small amount of electrical current?

Correct answer: The heart

ISED B-003-018-007

What is the lowest voltage that is usually considered hazardous to humans?

Correct answer: 30

ISED B-003-018-008

What should you do if you discover someone who is being burned by high voltage?

Correct answer: Turn off the power, call for emergency help and provide first aid if needed

ISED B-003-018-009

What is the safest method to remove an unconscious person from contact with a high-voltage source?

Correct answer: De-energize the power source before touching the person

ISED B-003-018-010

Before checking a fault in a mains-operated power supply unit, it would be safest to first:

Correct answer: turn off the power and unplug the power cord

ISED B-003-018-011

What is the risk involved in troubleshooting a live power supply?

lessons.title: Protective grounding, fuses and stored energy
lessons.teachingSummary: Ground and bond station equipment correctly. A mains protective-earth conductor, normally green in the bank's example, connects to the chassis to provide a fault-current path so protective devices can operate. A station single-point grounding arrangement and bonding between ground electrodes reduce dangerous voltage differences; separate isolated rods are not a substitute for proper bonding.
lessons.teaching:
Ground and bond station equipment correctly. A mains protective-earth conductor, normally green in the bank's example, connects to the chassis to provide a fault-current path so protective devices can operate. A station single-point grounding arrangement and bonding between ground electrodes reduce dangerous voltage differences; separate isolated rods are not a substitute for proper bonding.

A copper-clad steel rod combines conductivity with mechanical strength. At RF, even an ordinary-looking long ground wire can have high impedance: the bank's 10-m wire from a third-floor station can cause RF on the chassis and burns. RF grounding, protective earthing and lightning protection have related but distinct requirements.

Use the specified fuse current rating. A higher rating may leave wiring/equipment unprotected and permit fire. A fuse's voltage rating specifies the voltage it can interrupt without continuing to arc.

After disconnecting a supply, filter capacitors can remain charged. Qualified service procedures use an insulated discharge tool with an appropriate series resistor and verify the voltage before contact. Do not assume unplugging alone eliminates stored energy or use a bare screwdriver to discharge a capacitor.

ISED B-003-019-001

For best protection from electrical shock, what should be grounded in your station?

Correct answer: All station equipment

ISED B-003-019-002

Established practice demands that all ground electrodes be bonded together with heavy conductors. What protection does this provide in case of a lightning strike?

Correct answer: Prevents voltage differences between devices

ISED B-003-019-003

Why should you never use a fuse with a higher current rating than specified?

Correct answer: A fault may cause permanent damage, including a fire

ISED B-003-019-004

Which of these materials is best for a ground rod driven into the earth?

Correct answer: Copper-clad steel

ISED B-003-019-005

You need to work on a power supply that has been taken offline. What is the first thing you should do once the cabinet is open?

Correct answer: Discharge the filter capacitors

ISED B-003-019-006

Where should the green wire in a three-wire AC line cord be connected in a power supply?

Correct answer: To the chassis

ISED B-003-019-007

Your third-floor station has a ground wire running 10 metres down to a ground rod. You get an RF burn when you touch your HF transceiver while transmitting. What is the likely cause?

Correct answer: The ground wire has high impedance on your operating frequency

ISED B-003-019-008

Where should the chassis ground terminals on all station equipment be connected?

Correct answer: To the station's single-point ground

ISED B-003-019-009

What is a safe method to discharge power supply filter capacitors?

Correct answer: Use an insulated shorting stick with an inline resistor

ISED B-003-019-010

On mains-operated power supplies, the ground wire of the AC line is connected to the power supply chassis. What protection does this provide if a fault occurs in the power supply?

Correct answer: Ensures the chassis does not become energized

ISED B-003-019-011

Why do fuses have a voltage rating?

Correct answer: To specify the voltage that can be interrupted without arcing

lessons.title: Towers, lightning and safe antenna access
lessons.teachingSummary: Antenna work involves fall, falling-object, RF and electrical hazards. Use approved fall-arrest equipment and appropriate training for tower work; ground helpers need hard hats. Keep antennas and their possible fall paths clear of power lines. Before repairs, disable the transmitter and disconnect the feedline so no one can unexpectedly energize the antenna.
lessons.teaching:
Antenna work involves fall, falling-object, RF and electrical hazards. Use approved fall-arrest equipment and appropriate training for tower work; ground helpers need hard hats. Keep antennas and their possible fall paths clear of power lines. Before repairs, disable the transmitter and disconnect the feedline so no one can unexpectedly energize the antenna.

Install wire antennas high enough that people cannot touch any part from the ground. RF voltage can burn at an antenna or open-wire feedline. Ground-mounted antennas need appropriate exclusion distance/barriers while transmitting; a convenient low location does not make them safe to touch.

Bond/ground antenna and rotator cables using an appropriate system. A feedline surge protector belongs outside, close to the grounding/bonding arrangement. Disconnecting equipment from antenna cables and power lines provides the bank's best equipment protection when a station is not used. Plan this before a storm; do not handle outdoor conductors or disconnect exposed cables during nearby lightning.

ISED B-003-020-001

Why should you ground all antenna and rotator cables when your station is not in use?

Correct answer: To help protect the station equipment and building from lightning damage

ISED B-003-020-002

You want to install a lightning surge protector on your transmission line, where should it be inserted?

Correct answer: Outside, as close to earth grounding as possible

ISED B-003-020-003

How can your station equipment best be protected from lightning damage?

Correct answer: Disconnect all equipment from the power lines and antenna cables

ISED B-003-020-004

What equipment should be worn for working on an antenna tower?

Correct answer: Approved fall arrest equipment

ISED B-003-020-005

Why should you wear approved fall arrest equipment if you are working on an antenna tower?

Correct answer: To limit injuries if you fall

ISED B-003-020-006

For safety, how high should you place a horizontal wire antenna?

Correct answer: High enough so that no one can touch any part of it from the ground

ISED B-003-020-007

Why should you wear a hard hat if you are on the ground helping someone work on an antenna tower?

Correct answer: To protect your head from something dropped from the tower

ISED B-003-020-008

Why should your outside antennas be high enough so that no one can touch them while you are transmitting?

Correct answer: Touching the antenna might cause RF burns

ISED B-003-020-009

Why should you make sure that no one can touch an open-wire transmission line while you are transmitting with it?

Correct answer: Because high-voltage radio energy might burn the person

What safety precautions should you take before beginning repairs on an antenna?

Correct answer: Be sure to turn off the transmitter and disconnect the transmission line

ISED B-003-020-011

What safety precaution is especially important for a ground-mounted antenna?

Correct answer: Ensure people are kept at a safe distance

lessons.title: Reduce RF exposure with location and distance
lessons.teachingSummary: RF can heat body tissue; eyes are particularly vulnerable to heating. Keep a handheld's antenna away from your head and other people, especially while transmitting. Mount UHF/microwave antennas where people cannot approach the energized radiating structure, and prevent accidental power-up before removing an amplifier's shielding.
lessons.teaching:
RF can heat body tissue; eyes are particularly vulnerable to heating. Keep a handheld's antenna away from your head and other people, especially while transmitting. Mount UHF/microwave antennas where people cannot approach the energized radiating structure, and prevent accidental power-up before removing an amplifier's shielding.

In the ideal far field of a free-space source, power density falls with the square of distance. Doubling distance reduces it to one quarter; tripling reduces it to one ninth. This simple model does not describe every near-field or reflective indoor situation.

Place indoor antennas as far as practicable from occupied living space. Mount directional high-gain antennas so their main beams do not illuminate people in nearby structures. Keep both the ends and centre of dipoles high and inaccessible, since current/voltage distribution alone is not a reason to allow contact with another part of the antenna. Use the actual RF-exposure assessment as well as these good layout principles.

ISED B-003-021-001

What should you do for safety when operating at UHF and microwave frequencies?

Correct answer: Keep antenna away from your eyes when RF is applied

ISED B-003-021-002

What should you do for safety if you put up a UHF transmitting antenna?

Correct answer: Make sure the antenna will be in a place where no one can get near it when you are transmitting

ISED B-003-021-003

What should you do for safety, before removing the shielding on a UHF power amplifier?

Correct answer: Make sure the amplifier cannot accidentally be turned on

ISED B-003-021-004

Why should you make sure the antenna of a hand-held transceiver is not close to your head when transmitting?

Correct answer: To reduce your exposure to the radio frequency energy

ISED B-003-021-005

How should you position the antenna of a hand-held transceiver while you are transmitting?

Correct answer: Away from your head and away from others

ISED B-003-021-006

How can exposure to a large amount of RF energy affect body tissue?

Correct answer: It heats the tissue

ISED B-003-021-007

Which body organ is the most likely to be damaged from the heating effects of RF radiation?

Correct answer: Eyes

ISED B-003-021-008

How does the power density of an electromagnetic wave change as it propagates away from an antenna in free space?

Correct answer: It decreases as the square of the distance

ISED B-003-021-009

If you operate your station with indoor antennas, what precautions should you take when you install them?

Correct answer: Locate the antennas as far away as possible from living spaces that will be occupied while you are operating

Correct answer: As high as possible to prevent people from coming in contact with the antenna

exercises.prompt: A radio works on receive but its DC connector becomes hot on transmit. What do you check?
exercises.answer: Stop and inspect connector contact resistance, wire size, current rating, secure connections, voltage drop, and fuse arrangements. Transmit usually draws more current, revealing a weak connection.

exercises.prompt: Does a 1:1 SWR guarantee that standing next to the antenna is safe?
exercises.answer: No. RF exposure depends on transmitted power, frequency, duty cycle, gain, distance, and the field geometry. Match and exposure are different questions.

lessons.title: This is a cumulative chapter
lessons.body:
This chapter reviews the material taught in chapters 1–11. Its short mixed test can draw from any of the 984 official Basic questions, not just these review paragraphs. The prerequisite topic index below links to all 100 detailed lessons, including their worked examples and question-specific facts. Use it before the test whenever a subject is unfamiliar.

A full practice exam is a separate 100-question activity. Each full exam selects one question from every official topic group. The question bank, official answers and chapter pools are unchanged in this update; the teaching material has been expanded to match them.

lessons.title: Solve a calculation in five steps
lessons.body:
Identify the requested quantity, write the known values with units, choose and rearrange the formula, convert prefixes, then calculate. Finally check the direction of change: more resistance at a fixed voltage lowers current; doubling voltage at a fixed resistance quadruples power; a shorter wire resonates higher.

QuantityUseful relationship
Voltage, current, resistanceV = IR; I = V/R; R = V/I
DC powerP = VI = I²R = V²/R
Free-space wavelengthλ(m) ≈ 300/f(MHz)
HF wire dipole / quarter waveTotal dipole ≈ 143/f; quarter wave ≈ 71.3/f
Full wire-loop perimeterApproximately 306/f(MHz)
TransformerVoltage ratio = turns ratio; impedance ratio = turns ratio squared
Power in dB+3 ≈ ×2; +6 ≈ ×4; +10 = ×10

Read the wording carefully: a full dipole, one dipole leg, a loop perimeter and one side of a loop are different lengths. Similarly DC input, RF output, PEP, ERP and EIRP are different power quantities.

lessons.title: Read the question, especially NOT and minimum
lessons.body:
Before choosing an answer, identify whether the question asks for a true answer, a false statement, the minimum qualification, or the most suitable option among those listed. In the detailed lessons, false-statement selections are explicitly labelled false and followed by the true rule.

Compare Basic, Honours and Advanced privileges using the qualification lesson; installation and operating tasks can require different qualifications. For technical questions distinguish the job of a mixer, filter, amplifier and detector. For antennas distinguish resonance, impedance match, pattern and efficiency. For interference distinguish overload, audio rectification, harmonics and splatter. The topic index takes you directly to the full explanation for each distinction.

lessons.title: Prepare for the real examination
lessons.body:
Basic passes at 70%; Basic with Honours begins at 80%. The app stores each submitted practice attempt with its answers, so review mistakes, read the linked lesson, practise the relevant lab and try again after studying. Aim for several strong results on fresh full exams rather than memorizing answer letters.

The glossary is available from the persistent header on every screen. You may use it while learning or practising; for a realistic readiness check, try a complete exam without consulting it. The actual examiner determines the permitted reference aids, identity checks, format and accommodations. ISED provides labelled formula/block-diagram study material and an unlabelled permitted examination aid. A practice score never grants operating privileges.

Use the topic index below for the complete prerequisite readings. Your notes, completed chapters and earlier scores remain available as you review.

exercises.prompt: A 13.8 V radio draws 10 A. A 3 dB cable loss follows its 50 W RF output. Find DC input and approximate antenna input.
exercises.answer: DC input = 13.8 × 10 = 138 W. Antenna input ≈ 50 × 10^(−3/10) = 25.1 W. DC input, RF output, and cable-delivered power are different quantities.

exercises.prompt: A 14.2 MHz dipole is too short and your receiver hears a noisy 7 MHz band at midday. Which two independent ideas explain the observations?
exercises.answer: A short dipole tends to resonate above its target, so it needs more electrical length. Daylight D-region absorption can affect lower HF paths; received noise and propagation also depend on local sources and conditions.

glossary.definition: A sequence of audio tones used to address or identify a particular radio or group. The exact tone plan and code length depend on the system.
glossary.example: A selective-calling ID may be shown under OWNID on some radios.

glossary.definition: A common nominal impedance for radio connectors, coaxial feedlines and transceiver ports. It is not the same as measuring 50 Ω DC resistance across a length of coax.
A friendly amateur-radio closing meaning best regards.
AC changes direction periodically. DC maintains one direction, though its value can still vary. A typical radio power supply converts mains AC into low-voltage DC.
An ADC turns sampled analogue signals into digital values. A DAC produces an analogue output from digital values.
An additional Canadian amateur qualification associated with further technical and operating privileges. This app prepares for the Basic examination, with Honours as a study goal.
The receiver volume control: it adjusts audio delivered to headphones or a speaker.
glossary.example: Use AF gain for comfortable listening without changing the transmitter’s output.

glossary.definition: Automatic gain control; manages receiver gain as input levels change.
Automatic level control; limits transmitter drive or output to help prevent overdrive.
Encodes information by varying a carrier’s amplitude. Conventional AM contains the carrier plus upper and lower sidebands. Too much modulation can cause distortion and unwanted emissions.
glossary.example: Broadcast medium-wave radio commonly uses AM. At 100% modulation, an ideal AM envelope just reaches zero at its minima.

glossary.definition: The unit of electric current: the rate of electric charge flow.
glossary.example: A radio requiring 10 A needs a suitable supply, wiring and protection for that load.

glossary.definition: A signalling feature that sends a programmed unit identifier, often at the beginning or end of a transmission. Its implementation depends on the radio.
glossary.example: An ANI number in programming software and an amateur call sign serve different purposes.

glossary.definition: A matching network that transforms the impedance presented to a transmitter.
An amateur packet system for position reports, messages, telemetry and other real-time information. Its channels and operating practices depend on location.
Reduces the signal level entering a receiver. Can improve reception when very strong signals overload it.
A data-link protocol commonly used for amateur packet radio. Packets include addressing and error-detection information.
An interface between balanced and unbalanced systems; some also transform impedance.
The boundary of an allocated or authorized frequency band. The complete transmitted signal must fit within the applicable limits.
Recommended coordination of activities inside an allocation.
A signal’s occupied frequency range, or a device’s usable passband under specified conditions.

The entry Canadian amateur radio qualification. The Basic examination has 100 multiple-choice questions and a 70% pass mark. A new Basic-only result below 80% generally limits frequency access to amateur allocations above 30 MHz.

Basic examination achievement at 80% or higher, granting the additional frequency privileges specified by Canadian rules, including amateur allocations below 30 MHz. It does not by itself become the Advanced Qualification.
Symbols per second; not necessarily the same as bits per second.
Inhibits transmission when the radio detects a busy channel according to its programmed rules.
glossary.example: A radio that beeps instead of transmitting may have busy-channel lockout enabled.

glossary.definition: Beamwidth describes the angular width of a main lobe at a stated level, often half power. Front-to-back ratio compares radiation in the forward and opposite directions.
Beat-frequency oscillator; provides a reference for receiving CW and SSB.
A four-level digital modulation technique. In amateur radio it is associated with Yaesu System Fusion equipment; the modulation name and the complete system are different concepts.
The point in the measurement setup at which calibration defines the reference for the instrument’s readings.
glossary.example: Calibrate at the far end of a test cable when you want that cable removed from the antenna measurement.

glossary.definition: The station identifier assigned under the applicable radio authorization. In Canada, the required identification follows Canadian operating standards.
A component that stores energy in an electric field and opposes changes in voltage. Its capacitive reactance magnitude decreases with frequency.
An RF waveform used as a reference or modulated to carry information.
The travelling-wave voltage/current ratio set by a line’s geometry and materials.
An impedance intended to impede unwanted current, often common-mode current on the outside of a coaxial shield. A choke and an impedance-transforming balun are not automatically interchangeable.
Coaxial cable: an inner conductor surrounded by insulation and an outer conductor or shield. Frequently used as an unbalanced RF feedline.

DMR settings: the colour code is a system access parameter, while a time slot selects one of two alternating traffic slots on a typical two-slot DMR repeater. Matching them alone does not ensure every other setting is correct.
Current flowing on an unintended shared path, such as the outside of coax.
A conductor permits charge flow readily; an insulator resists it under the intended conditions. Real materials and insulation have limits.
Conductors providing a return-current system for certain antennas, especially verticals. Their size and placement affect impedance and efficiency.
A general invitation for any station to reply. Listen first and make sure the frequency is available.
glossary.example: On HF: CQ CQ, this is [your assigned call sign].

glossary.definition: A low-frequency continuous tone sent with an analogue FM signal. A receiver can require the matching tone before opening its speaker, and a repeater can require it for access. It provides neither privacy nor encryption.
glossary.example: A repeater listing might require a 100.0 Hz transmit tone. Tone encode sends it; tone decode requires it on receive.

glossary.definition: In amateur operation, CW usually means a carrier keyed on and off to send Morse code. The carrier is present during each dot or dash; controlled keying edges limit unwanted bandwidth.
glossary.example: Dots and dashes change how long the carrier is on. CW does not mean ordinary voice on an unmodulated carrier.

glossary.expansion: Digital Smart Technologies for Amateur Radio
glossary.definition: A digital voice and data system used on amateur radio. Uses callsign-oriented addressing and system-specific routing settings.
Decibel; a logarithmic ratio. Use 10 log for power.
Antenna gain referenced to a half-wave dipole.
Antenna gain referenced to an isotropic radiator.
An absolute power level expressed on a logarithmic scale. 0 dBm is 1 mW; 30 dBm is 1 W.
glossary.example: A value in dBm is a power level. A value in dB alone normally describes a ratio.

glossary.definition: A coded, low-rate digital signal carried with analogue FM audio to control access or receiver squelch. Radios must agree on the code and, where applicable, normal or inverted polarity. DCS does not turn analogue voice into digital voice and does not provide privacy.
glossary.example: D023N identifies a particular DCS code with normal polarity. It is not a 23 Hz CTCSS tone.

glossary.definition: A logarithmic ratio. For power, dB = 10 log10(P₂/P₁). About +3 dB doubles power and −3 dB halves it. Voltage ratios use 20 log10 only under appropriate equal-impedance conditions.
Recovers the information carried by a modulated signal. Different modes require appropriate demodulation.
A semiconductor component that conducts much more readily in one direction than the other. Used for rectification, switching and signal detection.
A balanced antenna with two conductive sides, often centre-fed and about half a wavelength long.
A digital radio standard used in amateur and commercial systems. Amateur configurations commonly use a Radio ID, talkgroup, colour code and time slot.
glossary.example: A DMR Radio ID and an ISED call sign are different identifiers.

glossary.definition: Mathematical processing of digitized signals for filtering, demodulation, noise reduction and related tasks.
Icom terminology for a digital coded squelch system in the DCS family. Use the correct code and polarity for the equipment involved.
glossary.example: A radio menu may say DTCS where another brand says DCS.

glossary.definition: A signalling method that sends a pair of audio tones for each key. Often used for selective calling or authorized repeater control.
glossary.example: The familiar telephone keypad uses DTMF tones.

glossary.definition: A power- and frequency-rated non-radiating RF load for testing.
Communication using different transmit and receive frequencies. Full duplex permits simultaneous transmit and receive; a typical handheld repeater user operates half duplex.
glossary.example: The repeater receives its input while transmitting its output.

glossary.definition: The fraction of time a transmitter or component is active over a stated interval. Thermal and exposure assessments depend on the relevant duty cycle.
glossary.example: A steady digital transmission may heat a transmitter differently from intermittent speech at the same peak setting.

glossary.definition: A distant station or long-distance contact. What counts as distant depends on the band and operating context.
Equivalent isotropically radiated power; combines antenna input power and gain relative to isotropic.
Effective radiated power; uses gain referenced to a half-wave dipole.
The unit of capacitance. Radio tuned circuits often use picofarads (pF), while power-supply capacitors may use microfarads (µF).
The point where a transmission line connects to an antenna. Feed-point impedance depends on the antenna and installation.
Passes some frequencies while attenuating others. Low-pass, high-pass, band-pass and band-reject describe different responses.
glossary.example: A low-pass filter may reduce transmitter harmonics above its passband.

glossary.definition: Encodes information by varying the instantaneous frequency of a carrier while its amplitude stays approximately constant. Commonly used for local VHF/UHF voice and repeaters.
glossary.example: Speech changes the frequency deviation. It should not intentionally change the RF envelope amplitude.

glossary.definition: A narrow-band, time-synchronized digital mode used for weak-signal amateur contacts. It exchanges short structured messages rather than ordinary voice.
A protective device that interrupts a circuit under specified overcurrent conditions. Its rating and placement must suit the wiring and equipment.
glossary.example: A fuse is not a guarantee against electric shock; never substitute a larger fuse to hide a fault.

glossary.definition: An increase in a signal level, or an antenna’s directional advantage relative to a stated reference. Amplifier gain describes amplification; antenna gain describes concentration of radiation. Always check whether the number is a power ratio, a voltage ratio, dBi or dBd.
glossary.example: An ideal antenna with 3 dB more gain gives about twice the power density in its main direction for the same applied power. It does not create transmitter power.

glossary.definition: A compact geographical locator used for reporting station position, often using the Maidenhead system. It describes a grid area rather than an exact street address.

Grounding provides connections to the applicable reference or earth system. Bonding joins conductive parts to reduce dangerous voltage differences. Safety ground, lightning protection and RF return paths have different functions and require appropriate design.
Propagation along the surface of the Earth.
A frequency that is an integer multiple of a fundamental.
The unit of inductance. RF coils commonly use microhenries (µH) or nanohenries (nH).
The unit of frequency, equal to one cycle per second.
glossary.example: 1 MHz = 1,000,000 Hz. A 100 Hz CTCSS tone is an audio signalling frequency, not the radio’s VHF carrier frequency.

glossary.definition: The 3–30 MHz frequency region. Several amateur bands lie here, and ionospheric propagation can support long-distance contacts.
glossary.example: The 14 MHz amateur band is in HF.

glossary.definition: Two signal components separated by a quarter cycle. Together they preserve amplitude and phase information used in SDR processing.
Intermediate frequency used after frequency conversion in a receiver or transmitter.
Resistance plus reactance, often written R + jX.
A component that stores energy in a magnetic field and opposes changes in current. Its inductive reactance increases with frequency.
Unwanted frequency combinations created by nonlinearity.
Upper-atmosphere regions containing charged particles that affect radio propagation. Their density changes with sunlight and other conditions.

glossary.expansion: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
glossary.definition: The federal department responsible for Canadian amateur radio certification and spectrum management.
An ideal point reference radiating equally in all directions.

The United Nations specialized agency coordinating international telecommunications matters, including international radio allocations and regulations. Canadian authorization still comes through Canadian rules.
The condition where inductive and capacitive reactances cancel.
A form of single-sideband modulation that keeps the sideband below the nominal suppressed-carrier frequency, with the other sideband and normally the carrier suppressed.
glossary.example: A 1 kHz audio tone on LSB at 7.100 MHz appears at 7.099 MHz.

glossary.definition: A saved set of radio settings, usually including receive frequency, transmit frequency or offset, mode and access signalling.
glossary.example: Two memories can have the same frequency but different tone settings.

glossary.definition: Prefixes express powers of ten: pico (p) = 10⁻¹², nano (n) = 10⁻⁹, micro (µ) = 10⁻⁶, milli (m) = 10⁻³, kilo (k) = 10³, mega (M) = 10⁶ and giga (G) = 10⁹.
glossary.example: 1 µF = 1,000 nF = 1,000,000 pF. Uppercase M and lowercase m differ by a factor of a billion.

glossary.definition: Adjusts how much microphone audio drives the transmitter. Excessive gain can cause distortion, over-deviation or splatter.
glossary.example: Use the transmitter’s meter and the manufacturer’s setup procedure rather than turning the control fully up.

glossary.definition: Combines signals in a nonlinear circuit to produce sum and difference frequency components. A receiver selects the desired component using filters.
glossary.example: A 14 MHz input mixed with a 9 MHz oscillator can produce components at 5 MHz and 23 MHz.

glossary.definition: Maximum usable frequency for a specified ionospheric path and conditions.
Path-dependent limits describing a usable HF propagation window under specified conditions. They change with ionization, absorption, noise and the chosen path.
A noise blanker targets certain impulse noise; noise reduction processes received signals to make background noise less distracting. Neither can recover information that has been completely lost.
The station coordinating a directed radio net. Follow its instructions for check-in and traffic handling.
An organized on-air meeting. A directed net has a net control station that coordinates participating stations.

FM configured for a narrower occupied bandwidth than a wider FM setting, usually by reducing frequency deviation and using appropriate audio filtering. It is still analogue FM. Match the channel plan and the other station’s deviation and bandwidth.
glossary.example: An NFM setting may use about ±2.5 kHz deviation on a suitably planned channel, but exact settings depend on the equipment and service. Narrow FM is not the same as turning down the speaker volume.

glossary.definition: Near-vertical incidence sky wave; high-angle HF for regional coverage.
The difference between a radio’s transmit and receive frequencies when using a repeater. Positive offset puts transmit above receive; negative offset puts it below.
glossary.example: 146.940 MHz receive with −0.600 MHz offset gives 146.340 MHz transmit.

glossary.definition: The unit of resistance and impedance. Ohm’s law relates voltage, current and resistance in a resistor.
glossary.example: 12 V across 6 Ω gives 2 A.

glossary.definition: For a resistor, voltage equals current multiplied by resistance: V = IR. Use consistent units.
glossary.example: At 12 V with 100 Ω, I = 0.12 A and resistor heat is 1.44 W.

glossary.definition: Radiates or receives broadly in all azimuth directions under specified conditions. It is not equal radiation in every three-dimensional direction.
glossary.example: A vertical antenna may have an approximately doughnut-shaped pattern, with weak radiation off its ends.

glossary.definition: An open circuit breaks the current path. A short circuit is an unintended or deliberately very low-impedance connection that can allow excessive current.
glossary.example: An open switch stops current; a short across a battery can create a high fault current.

glossary.definition: Produces a repeating electrical waveform. A radio uses oscillators to generate carriers, frequency references and local signals for conversion.
Overload occurs when a signal exceeds a receiver stage’s useful linear range. Desensitization is a loss of ability to hear weak signals, often in the presence of strong signals.
glossary.example: An attenuator can sometimes improve reception near very strong transmitters.

glossary.definition: A manufacturer-specific label for the radio’s own selective-calling identifier. In the Retevis RT95 manual, OWNID displays the current channel’s DTMF or 5-tone ID. Other radios may use the label differently; check that model’s manual. It is not automatically your amateur call sign or a DMR ID.
glossary.example: If an RT95 menu shows OWNID, it is asking about the programmed selective-calling ID, rather than antenna tuning or receiver gain.

glossary.definition: Digital communication that sends data in structured packets. A modem converts between data and a radio-compatible signal.
Peak envelope power; RF power at the peak of a modulation envelope.
The orientation or behaviour of the radio wave’s electric field.
An amplifier placed ahead of later receiver stages to boost weak signals. More preamplification can worsen overload when strong signals are present.
Digital modulation methods that encode information by changing phase or selecting different frequencies.
A button or control that changes a transceiver from receiving to transmitting while held.
glossary.example: Press PTT, pause briefly for a repeater to open, then speak clearly.

glossary.definition: A measure associated with energy storage compared with loss in a resonator. Higher Q generally means narrower fractional bandwidth near resonance.
Interference from other stations.
Atmospheric noise.
Higher-power operation, or a request to increase transmitter power. Applicable limits still depend on authorization and band rules.
Low-power operation. In contest contexts a common limit is 5 W output for CW, but definitions and categories vary.
Stop transmitting or close down the station.
Who is calling me? Also seen in the name of a callsign lookup service.
Signal fading: received strength varies with time.
Acknowledgement of reception; also a contact confirmation.
A radio contact or conversation between stations.
Change frequency.
Station location.
Electrical lengths equal to one-quarter or one-half of a wavelength. Actual element length depends on end effects, geometry and surrounding materials.
glossary.example: The wavelength lab compares free-space fractions with approximate practical wire lengths.

glossary.definition: The fraction of power accepted by an antenna that becomes radiated electromagnetic energy rather than loss. It is distinct from feedline loss and impedance mismatch.
glossary.example: A good match can still feed a very inefficient antenna.

glossary.definition: A numeric identifier used by some digital voice systems. Its assignment and format depend on the system. It does not replace the operator’s authorization or required station identification.
The frequency-dependent part of impedance caused by inductance or capacitance.
A rectifier changes AC into unidirectional current. A regulator maintains a desired output voltage within its operating limits. Filters reduce ripple.
A station that receives and retransmits to extend or facilitate communication.
Resistance is the real part of impedance and dissipates average power. Reactance is the imaginary part and comes from energy storage. Impedance combines both.
glossary.example: An impedance of 50 + j30 Ω has 50 Ω resistance and +30 Ω inductive reactance.

glossary.definition: A system of coloured bands indicating resistance and tolerance. Band count changes how many significant digits are used.
glossary.example: For a four-band resistor: first two bands are digits, third is a multiplier, fourth is tolerance.

glossary.definition: A condition where net reactance is approximately zero.
The reflected-power ratio expressed as a positive dB loss: larger return loss means less reflection and a better match.
glossary.example: A VNA may instead plot S11 magnitude in negative dB; a more negative value indicates less reflection.

glossary.definition: Radio frequency.
Adjusts amplification early in a receiver. Reducing it can help with overload or strong signals; it is different from the speaker volume control.
glossary.example: Turning AF gain down quiets the speaker. Turning RF gain down changes receiver amplification.

glossary.expansion: Radiocommunication Information Circular / Regulation by Reference
glossary.definition: ISED publication designations. RIC-3 describes amateur qualifications and syllabus information; RBR-4 contains amateur operating standards. Read current official versions when making operating decisions.
Shifts receive tuning slightly without changing the transmit frequency.
glossary.example: Use RIT to clarify an off-frequency SSB station while keeping your own transmit frequency fixed.

glossary.definition: An effective value of an alternating waveform used for power calculations. A sine wave’s RMS voltage is its peak voltage divided by √2.
Readability, signal strength, tone; voice normally uses R and S.
A text mode traditionally using frequency-shift keying and a teleprinter code.
A receiver indication of signal strength. Calibration varies between radios, especially on VHF/UHF; the reading is not a universal precision power measurement.
S11 describes input reflection. S21 describes forward transmission between two measurement ports under the stated reference conditions.
glossary.example: An antenna sweep commonly uses S11; a two-port filter test commonly uses S21.

glossary.definition: Health Canada’s radiofrequency exposure guidance. Station assessment must account for power, frequency, antenna characteristics, duty cycle and where people can be located.
glossary.example: A low SWR reading is not an RF-exposure assessment.

glossary.definition: A radio in which significant functions such as filtering or demodulation are performed by software. An SDR’s hardware tuning range does not grant permission to transmit.
glossary.example: A receive-only SDR can help you learn to recognize AM, FM and SSB signals.

glossary.definition: A receiver’s ability to reject unwanted nearby frequencies.
A receiver’s ability to detect weak signals.
Series components share one current path. Parallel components connect across the same two nodes and share the same voltage.
glossary.example: Two 100 Ω resistors in series give 200 Ω; in parallel they give 50 Ω.

glossary.definition: An exchange on one common frequency.

glossary.expansion: Signal plus noise plus distortion to noise plus distortion
glossary.definition: A receiver-quality measurement often used when specifying analogue FM sensitivity. The test conditions and bandwidth matter when comparing radios.
An area between usable ground-wave coverage and the first returning sky-wave coverage where a particular path may not be received.
Radio propagation refracted by the ionosphere back toward Earth.

Unwanted bandwidth caused by effects such as transmitter overdrive or abrupt waveform changes. Splatter is often associated with distorted speech modulation; key clicks with excessively abrupt CW keying.
An unwanted transmitted signal outside the intended emission, including certain harmonics and mixing products. Good transmitter design, adjustment and filtering help suppress it.
A common label for the squelch control in radio menus. It usually changes the threshold needed to unmute received audio.
Mutes receiver noise until a signal or matching signalling condition is detected. Setting the threshold too high can hide weak signals.
glossary.example: Carrier squelch responds to signal strength; tone squelch also requires a matching CTCSS or DCS setting.

glossary.definition: An amplitude-modulation technique that transmits one sideband while normally suppressing the carrier and the other sideband. USB and LSB are the two choices. It makes efficient use of bandwidth and transmitter power for voice.
glossary.example: Use a compatible USB or LSB receive setting to make an SSB voice signal intelligible.

glossary.definition: A receiver architecture that converts the tuned signal to one or more intermediate frequencies before demodulation.
The ratio of maximum to minimum voltage along a line with a standing wave. It indicates mismatch relative to a stated reference impedance. A low SWR alone does not prove efficient radiation.
glossary.example: 1:1 is a perfect impedance match. A dummy load can have low SWR while intentionally turning power into heat.

glossary.definition: A logical group address used by digital voice systems to route or select conversations.
Terminal node controller; interfaces digital data and a radio waveform.
Encode sends a CTCSS tone or DCS code. Decode requires a matching tone or code before the receiver opens squelch. You may need encode only for repeater access.
glossary.example: If you enable receive tone squelch with the wrong tone, you can miss an otherwise audible repeater.

glossary.definition: Limits the duration of one continuous transmission. Release PTT and follow the radio or repeater’s reset behaviour.
glossary.example: A time-out timer can limit an accidentally stuck microphone.

glossary.definition: Transfers energy between magnetically coupled windings. The turns ratio sets ideal voltage transformation and the square of that ratio relates impedances.
glossary.example: A 2:1 voltage turns ratio corresponds to a 4:1 impedance ratio.

glossary.definition: Semiconductor devices used for amplification or switching. In a bipolar transistor, base drive controls collector current; in a FET, gate voltage controls conduction.

Tuning can mean adjusting a radio’s frequency or changing antenna resonance. Impedance matching transforms a load to a desired input impedance. Antenna resonance and a 50 Ω match are related but distinct goals.
glossary.example: A resonant 100 Ω antenna has no reactive component at resonance, but its SWR on a 50 Ω line is 2:1.

glossary.definition: Ultra high frequency, 300–3000 MHz.
An impedance transformer between two unbalanced connections. Its ratio, power rating, bandwidth and common-mode behaviour depend on the design.

A form of single-sideband modulation that keeps the sideband above the nominal suppressed-carrier frequency. Normally the carrier and the lower sideband are suppressed. A receiver must use a compatible mode to reproduce intelligible speech.
glossary.example: A 1 kHz audio tone sent on USB at a nominal carrier of 14.200 MHz appears at 14.201 MHz. Here USB means upper sideband, not Universal Serial Bus.

glossary.definition: The common time reference used for radio logs and scheduled contacts. Local daylight-saving changes do not change UTC.
The wave speed in a transmission line divided by the speed of light in vacuum. It relates electrical wavelength to physical line length.
glossary.example: At velocity factor 0.66, one wavelength in the cable is about 66% of its free-space length.

glossary.definition: Originally an adjustable oscillator; on a modern radio, VFO mode usually means freely tuning a frequency instead of selecting a saved memory channel.
glossary.example: Choose VFO mode to enter a new receive frequency, then save its settings to a memory if desired.

glossary.definition: Very high frequency, 30–300 MHz.

glossary.expansion: Very high frequency / ultra high frequency
glossary.definition: VHF spans 30–300 MHz and UHF spans 300–3,000 MHz. These are frequency-region names; amateur allocations occupy particular parts of them.
Vector network analyzer; measures complex transmission and reflection.
The unit of electric potential difference. Voltage can drive current through an impedance.
glossary.example: 13.8 V DC is a common nominal supply for equipment designed for a 12 V vehicle electrical system.

glossary.definition: Automatically keys the transmitter when microphone audio passes a threshold. VOX gain or sensitivity sets the trigger level; delay sets how long the transmitter stays on after speech stops.
glossary.example: If room noise keeps keying the radio, reduce VOX sensitivity. Anti-VOX helps stop loudspeaker audio from triggering it.

glossary.definition: The voltage form of standing-wave ratio, often what an SWR meter or VNA reports.
The unit of power, or energy transferred per second. For a DC load, P = VI.
glossary.example: A 12 V load drawing 2 A consumes 24 W. RF output power and supply input power are different measurements.

glossary.definition: Distance travelled during one wave cycle, λ = c/f.
FM using wider deviation and occupied bandwidth than narrow-band voice FM. It is commonly associated with FM broadcast reception. It is not interchangeable with an amateur narrow FM channel setting.
Shifts transmit tuning slightly while leaving receive tuning unchanged. Exact labels vary by manufacturer.
Directional antenna using a driven element and parasitic reflector/director elements.

B-001-003-005.explanation: Select this because it is the false statement. Suspension is subject to the applicable notice and opportunity to make representations; do not memorize the selected wording as an unrestricted ministerial power.

B-001-003-006.explanation: Select this because it is false: an inspector does not have a general power to enter a dwelling with neither consent nor a warrant. The other choices describe conditions associated with authorized inspection.

B-001-006-005.explanation: This is the false statement. Amateur authority alone does not authorize aeronautical, marine or land-mobile operation. A separate service has its own licensing, certification and operator conditions.

B-001-022-001.explanation: This is the false fee statement: qualification examinations at an ISED office are free. An accredited examiner may separately recover their administration costs.

B-001-022-002.explanation: This is false. An accommodation can change the examination method, but does not excuse the candidate from demonstrating the required knowledge.

B-001-022-005.explanation: This is the false choice. The bank allows appropriate oral/adapted examination arrangements, not the described interpreter substitution for the examination language requirement.

B-001-007-003.explanation: This statement is false. Occasional business communications do not become permissible merely because the station normally makes personal amateur contacts.

B-002-006-007.explanation: One calibrated S-unit is 6 dB, a fourfold power change. 100/4 = 25 W.

B-002-006-008.explanation: Raising one calibrated S-unit requires +6 dB, or approximately four times the transmitter power.

B-002-009-007.explanation: Select this because it is false. A log is useful for confirming contacts and troubleshooting, but the bank does not make keeping it a regulatory requirement.

B-002-009-010.explanation: The stated offset is UTC−6: 19:00 minus six hours = 13:00, or 1 PM.

B-005-001-001.explanation: 1 MHz = 1000 kHz. Multiply 3.525 by 1000 to obtain 3525 kHz.

B-005-001-002.explanation: 1 A = 1000 mA. Divide 3000 mA by 1000 to obtain 3 A.

B-005-001-004.explanation: A microfarad is one million picofarads. Divide 1,000,000 pF by 1,000,000 to obtain 1 µF.

B-005-001-008.explanation: One quarter ampere is 0.25 A. Multiplying by 1000 gives 250 mA.

B-005-001-011.explanation: There are 1000 µH in 1 mH, so 10,000/1000 = 10 mH.

B-005-004-001.explanation: Use V = IR: 0.5 A × 2 Ω = 1.0 V.

B-005-004-006.explanation: First convert 10 mA to 0.010 A. R = 9/0.010 = 900 Ω.

B-005-004-009.explanation: Convert 200 mA to 0.200 A, then V = IR = 0.200 × 25 = 5 V.

B-005-004-011.explanation: Convert 300 mA to 0.300 A, then R = V/I = 3/0.300 = 10 Ω.

B-005-005-002.explanation: Each 100-Ω branch draws 12/100 = 0.12 A. Four parallel branches draw 4 × 0.12 = 0.48 A = 480 mA.

B-005-005-004.explanation: Each 1000-Ω branch draws 12/1000 = 0.012 A. Two branches draw 0.024 A = 24 mA.

B-005-005-006.explanation: Series resistances add: five × 10 Ω = 50 Ω.

B-005-005-007.explanation: Five equal 24-Ω resistors in series give 5 × 24 = 120 Ω.

B-005-005-009.explanation: For four equal parallel resistors, divide one resistance by four: 68/4 = 17 Ω.

B-005-005-010.explanation: Parallel branches have the same voltage. I = V/R means twice the current requires half the resistance.

B-005-006-002.explanation: The ideal minimum output power is V × I = 12 × 5 = 60 W. Real supply designs need additional margin.

B-005-006-003.explanation: 500 mA = 0.5 A. DC input power is 12 × 0.5 = 6 W.

B-005-006-004.explanation: The two equal series resistors share the heat equally. Each may dissipate 1 W, for 2 W total.

B-005-006-005.explanation: The equal parallel resistors share the power equally. Two 1-W ratings allow 2 W total under the stated conditions.

B-005-006-006.explanation: At unchanged resistance, P = V²/R. Doubling voltage multiplies power by 2² = 4.

B-005-006-007.explanation: Four equal 200-Ω parallel resistors make 200/4 = 50 Ω. Their 2-W ratings total 8 W, exceeding the required 5 W.

B-005-006-008.explanation: Rearrange P = VI into I = P/V: 30/12 = 2.5 A.

B-005-006-009.explanation: The series resistance is 10 + 10 = 20 Ω. P = V²/R = 100/20 = 5 W total.

B-005-008-004.explanation: 200 W to 20 W is a tenfold reduction, or −10 dB. Subtract 10 dB from S9+10 dB to obtain S9.

B-005-008-005.explanation: 150 W to 15 W removes 10 dB. S9+20 dB therefore becomes S9+10 dB.

B-005-008-009.explanation: 9 dB is approximately three 3-dB doublings: 2 W × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 W.

B-005-008-010.explanation: 6 dB loss is approximately division by four. 100/4 = 25 W.

B-005-008-011.explanation: A 30-dB reduction divides power by 1000: 100 W / 1000 = 0.1 W.

B-004-006-004.explanation: 10% of 100 Ω is 10 Ω. The allowed range is 100−10 to 100+10, or 90–110 Ω.

B-004-006-011.explanation: The first two bands make 27 and yellow is ×10⁴. Thus 27 × 10,000 = 270,000 Ω = 270 kΩ.

B-005-009-009.explanation: Two equal parallel inductors have half the individual inductance: 20/2 = 10 mH.

B-005-009-010.explanation: Two equal series capacitors have half the individual capacitance: 20/2 = 10 µF.

B-005-011-001.explanation: Neglecting losses, Iprimary = P/V = 250/120 ≈ 2.08 A, rounded to 2.1 A.

B-005-011-003.explanation: Input power is 120 × 0.5 = 60 W. At a 12-V secondary, I = 60/12 = 5 A.

B-005-011-004.explanation: The turns ratio is 500/250 = 2. Multiply the 120-V input by two to get 240 V.

B-005-011-007.explanation: An ideal 10-W output at 5 V supplies I = P/V = 10/5 = 2 A.

B-005-011-008.explanation: Voltage steps up by five, so current steps down by five. Primary current is 5 × 50 mA = 250 mA.

B-003-011-007.explanation: Conventional AM occupies both sidebands, so bandwidth is twice the highest audio frequency: 2 × 3 kHz = 6 kHz.

B-003-011-010.explanation: The difference is heat: 200 W DC input − 125 W RF output = 75 W of dissipation.

B-003-012-010.explanation: 1000 Hz is 1 kHz. Lower sideband places the tone below the suppressed carrier: 7100−1 = 7099 kHz.

B-003-010-006.explanation: For high-side injection, oscillator = receive frequency + IF. 3.540 MHz + 0.455 MHz = 3.995 MHz.

B-003-016-009.explanation: Parallel matching batteries retain 12 V and add capacity: 20 + 20 = 40 Ah.

B-003-016-010.explanation: Series batteries add voltage, 12 + 12 = 24 V, while retaining the 20-Ah capacity.

B-003-017-009.explanation: The 3-m separation means 6 m of supply-and-return conductor. 6 × 0.07 V/m = 0.42 V, under the 0.5-V limit.

B-006-008-003.explanation: Use λ = 300/f with f in MHz: 300/25 = 12 m.

B-006-009-011.explanation: Subtract the dipole-over-isotropic reference: 4.1 dBi − 2.1 dB = 2.0 dBd.

B-006-010-002.explanation: For this HF quarter-wave approximation, length = 71.3/21.125 ≈ 3.37 m.

B-006-010-003.explanation: The approximate free-space half wavelength is 150/223 m ≈ 0.673 m = 67 cm.

B-006-011-003.explanation: The director is shorter than the driven element. Use about 136/21.1 ≈ 6.44 m for the bank’s choice.

B-006-011-004.explanation: The reflector is longer. Use about 150/28.1 ≈ 5.34 m.

B-006-011-011.explanation: Ideal stacking adds roughly 3 dB, so 10 dBi + 3 dB = 13 dBi, before real feed losses.

B-006-012-001.explanation: The total HF dipole length is 143/28.150 ≈ 5.08 m; each leg is half of that.

B-006-012-009.explanation: Total HF dipole length is 143/3.75 ≈ 38.13 m.

B-006-013-003.explanation: Use the loop perimeter approximation 306/21.4 ≈ 14.30 m; this is all four sides together.

B-006-013-005.explanation: Delta-loop perimeter = 306/28.7 ≈ 10.66 m; it is not the length of one triangular side.

B-006-006-011.explanation: The required impedance ratio is 300/50 = 6:1. Do not confuse this with the turns ratio, which is its square root.

B-008-004-005.explanation: 21.375/7.125 = 3, identifying a third harmonic of the intended fundamental.

B-008-004-007.explanation: A 15-metre signal near 21 MHz has a third harmonic near 63 MHz, inside the stated TV channel.

B-008-004-010.explanation: A 10-metre transmission near 28 MHz has a second harmonic at 2 × 28 = 56 MHz.

B-001-023-001.explanation: This is false. Consult the applicable local/ISED process and determine whether a defined exclusion applies. Amateur certification is not an unconditional permission for structures of any size.

B-001-023-005.explanation: The question asks for the item that is NOT a required element of the default process. Written notice, a comment opportunity and responding to reasonable/relevant concerns are required; a public meeting is not automatically required.

B-001-024-008.explanation: This statement is false: handheld transmitters are not excluded from RF-exposure requirements. Exposure depends on the actual operating arrangement, not just the equipment category.

B-001-024-010.explanation: This is false. Safety Code 6 limits exposure quantities, such as fields, currents and energy absorption. Transmitter watts alone do not determine exposure.
